input: The warehouse extension has a net present value of $733k on the estimates the appraisal rests on. The installed cost is $1489k. The expected net saving is $265k per year for 12 years, and at a discount rate of 6% the present value of the savings is $2222k. The net present value is the present value of the savings less the installed cost, $2222k less $1489k, which gives the stated $733k. The appraisal discounts each year's saving at the same rate of 6% and adds the discounted savings over the 12 years before setting the total against the installed cost, which is treated as spent at the start. The appraisal period is the 12 years over which the savings are projected; nothing in the appraisal values the extension beyond that period. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the figures that decide the appraisal, the annual saving of $265k and the present value of $2222k built from it, are estimates throughout, and the installed cost of $1489k is the only figure in the appraisal that is a price rather than a forecast. The net present value of $733k is therefore as firm as the savings estimates and no firmer: if the realised saving falls short of $265k per year, the present value falls with it, and the margin of $733k is the amount by which the estimates can deteriorate before the appraisal turns. A measured saving on a comparable installation is the evidence that would settle the question the appraisal leaves open.
